sections.section_title: The Transition from Earth to Heaven
sections.summary: John hears the same trumpet-voice from 1:10 summoning him through an open door in heaven to see 'what must take place after these things,' with the phrase 'ha dei genesthai' (divine necessity) linking the opening commission (1:1, 1:19) to the beginning of the heavenly vision and establishing that the coming events are the outworking of God's determined purpose.

sections.section_title: The Throne and the One Seated
sections.summary: John is instantly 'in the Spirit' and sees a throne already established in heaven with a figure seated on it, described only by position rather than by name, following the biblical tradition of restraint in directly describing God's person seen in Ezekiel 1:26 and Daniel 7:9.

sections.section_title: The Appearance of the One Seated
sections.summary: The one on the throne is described as pure luminosity through precious stones -- jasper and sardius corresponding to the first and last stones of the high priest's breastplate encompassing all twelve tribes -- and a full-circle emerald rainbow encircling the throne, evoking God's covenant with Noah (Genesis 9:12-17) and Ezekiel's throne-glory (Ezekiel 1:28) as a visible sign of covenant faithfulness.

Twenty-four thrones encircle the central throne, occupied by twenty-four elders in white garments and golden victor-crowns (stephanoi), most naturally corresponding to the twenty-four priestly courses of 1 Chronicles 24, already possessing what the assemblies in chapters 2-3 were promised for conquering -- white garments (3:4-5), crowns of life (2:10), and thrones (3:21).

sections.section_title: Lightning, Thunder, and the Seven Spirits
sections.summary: Lightning, sounds, and thunder proceed continuously from the throne in present-tense emanation, drawn from the Sinai theophany (Exodus 19:16), while seven lamps of fire burning before the throne are explicitly identified as the seven spirits of God first mentioned in 1:4, evoking the temple menorah and Zechariah's lampstand vision (Zechariah 4:1-6, 10) as the visible manifestation of God's Spirit in its fullness.

Before the throne lies 'something like a sea of glass, like crystal,' described with double approximation, converging the Sinai pavement beneath God's feet (Exodus 24:10), Ezekiel's crystal-like expanse above the living creatures (Ezekiel 1:22), and the bronze sea of Solomon's temple used for priestly purification (1 Kings 7:23-26) -- now solid, transparent, and stable rather than liquid, suggesting purification completed.

Four living creatures (zoa, defined by life, distinct from theria/beasts) occupy the innermost position around the throne, full of eyes front, behind, around, and within, combining Ezekiel's four-faced cherubim (with faces distributed one per creature rather than all four on each) with Isaiah's six-winged seraphim, representing the fullness of created life -- lion, calf, man, eagle -- gathered as immediate attendants of the divine presence with exhaustive, all-directional perception.

The four living creatures ceaselessly declare the trisagion drawn from Isaiah 6:3 -- 'Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty, who was and who is and who is to come' -- combining the threefold superlative of absolute holiness with the title pantokrator (sovereign power over all things) and the dynamic expansion of the divine name from Exodus 3:14 across past, present, and arriving future, constituting the theological anchor of the entire vision.

sections.section_title: The Worship Cycle -- The Elders' Response
sections.summary: In an eternal liturgical cycle triggered by the creatures' worship, the twenty-four elders prostrate themselves and cast their crowns before the throne, declaring God 'worthy' (axios) to receive glory, honor, and power because he created all things and 'because of Your will they existed and were created' (dia to thelema sou), grounding God's sovereignty in his identity as Creator -- the first of two pillars of divine authority, the second being the Lamb's redemptive worthiness established in chapter 5.
